Abstract 23

REBCO-based superconducting magnets are considered crucial to the long-awaited realization of 24 commercially viable controlled thermonuclear fusion via compact reactor architectures. To expand the 25 current understanding of how the inherently reduced shielding of these proposed designs affects the 26 radiation-sensitive high temperature superconductors, the activation spectra and microstructure of 27 REBCO tapes irradiated more traditionally with fission-reactor neutrons were compared to those 28 irradiated with the higher-fidelity fusion-like spectrum produced by thick target deuteron breakup in a 29 first-of-its-kind irradiation experiment on these coated conductors. For the fusion-like case, several peaks 30 in the activation spectrum confirmed high-threshold nuclear reactions, and SEM revealed superficial 31 alterations to the most intensely irradiated area. TEM revealed that although both sets of microstructures 32 appeared strained, the 14 MeV-irradiated damage manifested as milder patches of subcascades and large 33 voids, with no large amorphous clusters classically associated with REBCO fission irradiations, as 34 confirmed by our own fission samples. Computational analysis on the visually indistinguishable respective 35 lattice strains revealed comparable damage metrics of the fusion-like samples to fission samples, despite 36 the much lower total fluences on the former. The nuclear physics origins of these findings and their 37 implications for the superconducting properties are also discussed. These results present an important 38 preliminary step in the rigorous technical readiness qualifications required by this pivotal technology in 39 the burgeoning REBCO-based compact fusion industry. 40

Introduction 41

Fusion, a promising, but so-far commercially unachieved source of clean energy [1], may be realized in 42

the near future by utilizing Rare-Earth Barium Copper Oxide (REBCO) coated conductors as the high- 43

temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets in tested and proven reactor architectures like the tokamak 44

or stellarator [2], [3]. These compact designs are aimed at being smaller, and therefore quicker to build 45

and more cost effective than the world’s leading fusion project, the International Thermonuclear 46

Experimental Reactor (ITER), whose toroidal field coils are based on more traditional low-temperature 47

superconductors (LTS) to confine the plasma during operation [4]. A major consequence of compact 48

designs is the increased radiation exposure from the plasma on the surrounding materials due to the 49

reduced room for shielding. The intense radiation may have a particularly disabling effect on the toroidal 50

field (TF) magnets [5], among other components. These effects include displacement damage, activation, 51

transmutation, gas production, swelling, embrittlement, and irradiation-induced creep [6], [7]. Besides 52

compromising mechanical properties, these can also affect the superconductor performance by altering 53

the pinning landscape and therefore vortex dynamics of REBCO [8]. 54

Interestingly, the change in the key superconducting parameter of critical current (Jc) has been shown 55

to undergo a complex variation, rather than a trivial monotonic decrease that one would imply from first 56

principles [9]. Studies attempting to replicate the effects of fusion reactor conditions on REBCO do show 57

that irradiation results in the formation of additional irradiation-induced artificial pinning centers (APCs) 58

[10]. This change in microstructure appears to have two competing effects on the overall Jc in these type- 59

II superconductors: an initial, ostensibly parabolic increase from enhanced vortex pinning until some 60

critical point of defect-density saturation, and a simultaneous linear decrease due to copper oxide plane 61

and chain damage [11]. Since the former is proportionally greater than the latter, at first the new APCs 62

benefit the net Jc, but eventually, as this benefit attenuates, the overall critical current begins to trend 63

downward and is suppressed altogether at some critical fluence. Understanding the rate and nature of 64

this variation and ultimate degradation is therefore crucial for the eventual implementation and 65

commercial success of REBCO-based compact fusion plants. 66

While some irradiation studies have been performed on REBCO, they have mostly relied on ions Error! 67 Reference source not found., [13], or fission reactor neutrons [14], [15] that have generally softer neutron 68

spectra when compared to what can be expected at the magnet location for compact fusion reactors [5]. 69

This study aimed to expand upon the known materials-focused literature by conducting thick target 70

deuteron breakup (TTDB) neutron irradiations, which can deliver the harder, 14-MeV-dominated, fusion- 71

like spectrum we anticipate in-service. We began by following up on a study by coauthor Iio et al. [16], 72

examining their ‘used’ fission-irradiated and transport-measured samples, now through the lens of 73

materials science. Following previously unreported TTDB irradiations on these modern coated conductors, 74

we compared the fission samples with the fusion-like neutron-irradiated ones using radionuclide analysis, 75

scanning and transmission electron microscopy, and computational analysis. 76

Neutron Activation Analysis confirms high-threshold inelastic reactions 79

The activation gamma spectra for both SuperPower and Fujikura BR2 samples are shown in Fig. 1a, and 80 Fig. 1b, respectively, both exhibiting several prominent peaks. As detailed in the methods section, the 81 samples are labeled by their make (SCS for SuperPower, FYSC for Fujikura), method of irradiation (BR2 for 82 Belgian Reactor 2/fission neutrons, 88-Inch for 88-Inch Cyclotron/fusion-like neutrons), and dose (‘P’ for 83

pristine/unirradiated, ‘LD’ for the lower fission dose of 8.23×1021 n/m2, ‘HD’ for the higher fission dose 84

7.92×1022 n/m2, ‘C1’ for the lower fusion-like dose 6×1016 n/m2, and ‘C2’ for the higher fusion-like dose 85

6×1017 n/m2). Also note that BR2 samples where assayed 3 years after irradiation, while the 88-Inch 86 samples were done within hours of irradiation. For BR2 samples, the peak positions between SuperPower 87 and Fujikura spectra differ by less than 1 keV in most cases, which falls within the expected energy 88 resolution limits of standard gamma detectors. The activation gamma spectrum for an SCS-88-Inch-C1 89 sample positioned between 14° and 68° of the central 14 MeV cone (see methods) is shown in Fig. 1c and 90 Fig. 1d, also with prominent peaks identified and labeled. 91

For the BR2 gamma spectra, the most intense peaks were observed at 1174 keV and 1332 keV, 92 corresponding to the decay of cobalt-60 (⁶⁰Co), which is produced via reactions such as neutron capture 93 on nickel ⁵⁹Ni(n,γ)⁶⁰Ni followed by β⁻ decay, and 63Cu(n,α)⁶⁰Co, with zero-threshold 59Co(n,γ) radiative 94 capture contributing via moderated neutrons later in the cascade. This is expected given the high nickel 95 content in the Hastelloy substrate. The ⁶⁰Co peaks for the Fujikura samples were relatively higher 96 compared to the SuperPower samples, possibly due to the substrate thickness of the former being 50% 97 greater than that of the latter. In fact, if we account for the copper, the FYSC-SCH04 tapes are ~20% 98 thicker than the SCS-4050AP tapes, corroborated well by the ~25% higher activity of the Fujikura 99 samples, as reported in Table 1. Though the ⁶⁰Co peaks are indicative of reaction thresholds around 1– 100 2 MeV expected of fission spectra, we also see a 137Cs peak, indicative of high-threshold reactions such as 101 the 137Ba(n,p)137Cs channel which opens up ~7–8 MeV. The 137Cs peak persists relative to the ⁶⁰Co peak 102 due to the former’s longer half-life of 30.05 y compared to 5.27 y of the latter. Collectively, these results 103 support the conclusion that both thermal and fast neutron-induced reactions contributed to the observed 104 activation products. This reflects the characteristic mixed neutron energy spectrum of the BR2 reactor, 105 typical of fission sources, with two dominant components: a thermal peak below 0.1 eV and a fast peak 106 around ~1–2 MeV. 107

For the 88-Inch REBCO samples irradiated with a 14-MeV-peaked spectrum, however, an evidently 108 different activation profile is observed. The resulting gamma spectrum shows a prominent shift in both 109 the radionuclides produced and the scaled relative peak intensities, compared to the BR2’s fission- 110 spectrum activation. Notably, high-threshold reactions such as 138Ba(n,np)137Cs, 63Cu(n,α)60Co, and 111

62Ni(n,α)59Fe dominate, consistent with the hard neutron energy distribution favoring (n,2n) and (n,α) 112 channels. Strong features such as the 88Y lines at 898 and 1835 keV underscore this energy dependence, 113 as well as highlight the capacity of this Rare-Earth for neutron multiplication. The latter is striking since it 114 means that the yttrium, which sits at the heart of the necessarily highly-ordered modified-perovskite 115 superconductor unit cell, has the ability to release neutrons energetic enough to result in cascades of their 116 own. Though any initial 88Y signature in the BR2 samples would have decayed beyond detectability due to 117 the 106.6-day half-life, the same could not be said about the 137Cs signature, since its 30-year half-life 118 would have resulted in a peak which persisted by the time the measurement was made. In fact, despite 119 the relative scarcity of neutrons energetic enough to overcome this threshold, the signature is prominent 120 in the BR2 samples because the substantially larger total irradiation fluence compensates for this. In other 121 words, the 137Cs peak in the BR2 samples are due to the larger fluence and long half-life, whereas in the 122 88-Inch samples it is due to the harder neutron spectrum. The 138Ba(n,np)137Cs reaction is well-known to 123 have a high energetic threshold ~11.23 MeV, and is an example of a true disparity between the effects 124 of the fission and fusion-like spectra. Overall, these benchmark nuclear data experiments are crucial for 125 enabling high-fidelity Monte Carlo simulations of these superconductors for compact fusion reactor 126 engineers worldwide. 127

SEM shows thermomechanical degradation of REBCO tapes under direct beam irradiation 134

*Figure 2 shows side-by-side SEM of the exposed REBCO layers of pristine and neutron-irradiated 135*

samples. Aside from the central beam-spot irradiated area (discussed below), etched surfaces essentially 136

looked indistinguishable from their pristine counterparts, all matching the classic SEM of REBCO coated- 137

conductors in literature [17]–[19]. As exemplified by the pristine sample in Fig. 2a, typical SEM 138

micrographs (ab-plane coincident with image plane, c-axis out of page/screen) show the highly-textured 139

REBCO pseudo-single-crystal (dark background) populated by a few classic defects: usually porosity, Cu-O 140

or Ba-Cu-O grains (light circular precipitates), and so-called a-axis grains (square/rectangular objects), 141

which are still REBCO grains—though highly misoriented—where the a-axis of unit cell aligns normal to 142 the ab-planar surface instead of the c-axis. The defects present—as well as their size, density, and spatial 143 distribution—depend on parameters such as the thickness to which the REBCO layer is grown and the 144 dopant mol % used to form the APCs (which as mentioned enhance vortex pinning/critical current), and 145 typically vary extensively. Even for the highest-dose samples of each irradiation type shown in Figs. 4b– 146 4d, all defects and their relative densities appeared typical for REBCO. 147

However, the 88-Inch samples positioned near/coincident with the beam spot ∼0° were uniquely 148

affected, resulting in a few key superficial alterations. In Fig. 2e, we see an SEM image of the exposed 149

REBCO layer in the region directly impacted by the beam, including its less-affected borders. The region 150

within the white dashed lines outline the most intensely affected area, which exhibited altered relief and 151

compromised electrical conductivity, as evidenced by the charging visible. Along the boundary, other 152

distinct features are observed, including swelling (Fig. 2f) and a polygonal cellular surface pattern (Fig. 2g). 153

The unique microstructural changes observed in the beam-spot-aligned sample could be relevant to 154

REBCO positioned directly in-line with the diverter of a compact tokamak, which is expected to see 155

substantially higher fluxes relative to other segments along the TF D-coil [5], and is worth some brief 156 discourse. As shown in the higher magnification SEM in Fig. 2h, the polygonal pattern superficially 157

resembles grains, but it is unlikely to reflect the underlying REBCO texture, as the true grains in epitaxial 158

REBCO films are sub-micrometer in scale. Instead, the observed cellular relief is consistent with the 159

intrinsic MOCVD colony morphology of the REBCO thin film. It may be postulated that local overheating 160

during irradiation thermally induced surface etching, thereby enhancing the surface relief—via vacancy- 161

driven grooving and minor oxygen loss—ultimately sharpening the apparent cellular patterns that 162

represent the coalesced growth islands containing the true columnar grains of REBCO. 163

Similar patterns for thermally etched ceramics like Yttria-Stabilized Zirconia (YSZ) are also noted in 177

As for the result on the relief of the thin film, several theories were discussed, including irradiation- 181

induced transmutation blistering and eutectic/liquid-metal attack with subsequent cavitation and cap 182

rupture. Given the irradiation conditions—10 µC of 40 MeV deuterons fully stopped in a 7 mm Be breakup 183

target in direct contact with the REBCO tape over a 60 second exposure—the observed surface features 184

cannot be attributed to hydrogen or helium blistering, as the neutron fluence of ~10¹⁶ nm⁻² and implanted 185

deuteron dose are several orders of magnitude below known blistering thresholds in ceramics [21]. The 186

idea of eutectic or liquid-metal attack was entertained but ultimately discarded too since Ag–Ni/Hastelloy 187

systems lack a low-temperature eutectic and the calculated beam heating is insufficient to reach the 188

melting point of Ag. Instead, simple thermal modeling shows that localized beam energy deposition could 189

raise the beryllium and adjacent REBCO/silver stack by several hundred degrees Celsius. Such transient 190

overheating is sufficient to induce Ag thinning and partial dewetting, REBCO oxygen loss, and interfacial 191

delamination, consistent with the dark streaks and rumpled morphology observed upon visual inspection. 192

The damage is therefore best explained as thermomechanical degradation driven by transient beam 193

heating, not irradiation-induced gas blistering or eutectic interaction. 194

Sources of Error 496

All computational analysis occurs downstream from sampling and imaging, thus any upstream flaws may 497 lead to analytical errors. Possible sources of error at the sampling level include non-uniform lamella 498 preparation and differences in local thickness. At the imaging level, errors may arise from inconsistent 499 illumination and contrast, repeated tiles from the same region (which risks pseudoreplication), and spatial 500 bias (e.g. over-representation of defect-rich zones in the data). Many processing steps rely on fixed 501 parameter values, such as fixed-radius morphological operations, minimum length cutoffs, and, in 502 particular, mask designs and parameters. We mitigate these sources of error by carefully tuning any 503 parameters to match the data, however poor parameter selection would affect the results. Additionally, 504 while per-image medians reduce sensitivity to outliers and fragmentation they do not eliminate them 505 entirely. Analyses based on 12 and bootstrap confidence intervals assume that images are independent, 506 an assumption which may be violated if many tiles come from a single micrograph or area on a sample. 507 Finally, unequal group sizes can introduce biases when comparing groups. We also note that for the PCA 508 analysis, the code largely identified the atomic fringes as the principal component, analogous to ࢍࢉ iFFT 509 bands but sometimes did identify in-plane registry more analogous to ࢍࢇ࢈ iFFT bands. While this signature 510 does have consequences on the angular dispersion, the effect itself was clearly enhanced for irradiated 511 REBCO micrographs. In other words, the reported angular dispersions do reflect irradiation-induced 512 changes to the REBCO lattice, albeit partially indirectly since the damaged microstructure resulted in a 513 proportionally higher detection of ab-like principal components. 514
